power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

For the list of terms used to identifify marginally significant results, see this [blog post by Matthew Hankins](https://web.archive.org/web/20251001114321/https://mchankins.wordpress.com/2013/04/21/still-not-significant-2/). :::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p < .05", Text = "If the trend was significant (p < .05), it was removed using Theil-Sen regression before Tau was computed; otherwise, Tau was computed without correction."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = "p = .35", Sentence = "Adding random slopes did not improve model fit (χ²(2) = 2.10, p = .35); given the small number of participants, this does not indicate homogeneous treatment response."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. :::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1719 columns across 22 data files.
#### Issues Identified

74 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Spreadsheet formatting such as colour, merged cells, and blank rows/columns is not preserved when data are read programmatically or exported to CSV. Store data as a plain rectangular table (one header row, one column per variable, no colour-encoded meaning) so it is machine-readable.
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 22 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 9 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:9, File = c("Code POINT-Pain_Part1.Rmd", 
"Code POINT-Pain_Part2.Rmd", "Evaluation_revision_data_secure.Rmd", 
"Practitioner Validation_Analyses.Rmd", "Analyses_phase 1.Rmd", 
"Analyses_phase 2.Rmd", "ProCEss aids_analyses.Rmd", "Analyses_phase 3.Rmd", 
"ProCEss_main evaluation_analyses_data security.Rmd"), "Runs after" = c("—", 
"—", "—", "—", "Practitioner Validation_Analyses.Rmd", 
"Practitioner Validation_Analyses.Rmd", "Practitioner Validation_Analyses.Rmd", 
"ProCEss aids_analyses.Rmd", "—"), Basis = c("numeric", "numeric", 
"none", "none", "dependency", "dependency", "dependency", "dependency", 
"none")), row.names = c(NA, -9L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths

**5 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `SELECT_PATHWAY/main_data_evaluation.RData` to `main_data_evaluation.RData` (in ProCEss_main evaluation_analyses_data security.Rmd); `Phase_2.xlsx` to `../Data/Datasets/Phase_2.xlsx` (in Analyses_phase 2.Rmd); `Phase_1.xlsx` to `../Data/Datasets/Phase_1.xlsx` (in Analyses_phase 2.Rmd); `Phase_3.xlsx` to `../Data/Datasets/Phase_3.xlsx` (in Analyses_phase 3.Rmd); `Phase_1.xlsx` to `../Data/Datasets/Phase_1.xlsx` (in Analyses_phase 1.Rmd). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.
#### Files the deposit does not hold
The scripts that did not run through read 1 data file that is not in the deposit, and no script of the deposit writes: `output_pre-post-fu_summarised.csv`.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 9 scripts: 1 ran without error, 2 errored, 0 timed out, 1 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **5 scripts need a person** to choose a file, answer a question or use an app, which cannot be reproduced without one: Practitioner Validation_Analyses.Rmd, Analyses_phase 1.Rmd, Analyses_phase 2.Rmd, ProCEss aids_analyses.Rmd, Analyses_phase 3.Rmd. Naming the file in the script solves this. **4 scripts use an object or function that only another script defines**, so in the second run that script was loaded first, in the same session: `Analyses_phase 1.Rmd` after `Practitioner Validation_Analyses.Rmd`; `Analyses_phase 2.Rmd` after `Practitioner Validation_Analyses.Rmd`; `Analyses_phase 3.Rmd` after `ProCEss aids_analyses.Rmd`; `ProCEss aids_analyses.Rmd` after `Practitioner Validation_Analyses.Rmd`. Such a script should `source()` the other itself, since it does not run on its own. 

*a script hit an `object '...' not found` error, indicating it expected a variable another script defines. We inferred which script supplies it and re-ordered so that script runs first, and re-ran once. The outcomes above are from that corrected run.*

```{r}
), Outcome = c("dependency_unavailable", "errored", "ran_ok",

```
**Dependency-unavailable errors**

**1 script could not run because its own dependency is unavailable** — the package failed to install from both live CRAN and the CRAN Archive (or a GitHub/URL source could not be resolved). This is an infrastructure limitation, not a defect in the paper's code, so it does **not** force the traffic light red.

````
> hedges_g <- function(score, phase) {
>   a <- score[phase == 0 & !is.na(score)]   # baseline
>   b <- score[phase == 1 & !is.na(score)]   # treatment
>   nA <- length(a); nB <- length(b)
>   s_pool <- sqrt(((nA - 1) * var(a) + (nB - 1) * var(b)) / (nA + nB - 2))
>   d <- (mean(b) - mean(a)) / s_pool
>   J <- 1 - 3 / (4 * (nA + nB - 2) - 1)
>   tibble(n_baseline = nA, n_treatment = nB, hedges_g = J * d)
> }
````

text.text: Such decisions are often guided by clinical intuition and theoretical models, which are prone to systematic biases (Lutz et al., 2022; Meehl, 1954; Tversky & Kahneman, 1974).

text.text: For instance, optimism bias can affect how therapists evaluate their own performance and their patients' progress (Kaiser et al., 2022; Walfish et al., 2012).

text.text: Consequently, personalized approaches should be informed by individual patient data to select dose, sequencing, and adaptation of interventions, complementing rather than replacing clinical judgment (Lutz et al., 2022).

text.text: Recent methodological advances offer promising avenues to support individualized clinical decision-making in psychotherapy.

Ambulatory Assessment 1 , or Ecological 1 "Ambulatory assessment" is an umbrella term that encompasses passive sensing, ecological momentary assessment (EMA) and experience sampling methodology (ESM).
The latter two terms originate from different research traditions, both describing the sampling of subjective experiences and individual behaviors.
In the present study, we use EMA to describe repeated assessments of experiences and behaviors.
Momentary Assessment (EMA), enables repeated measurement of psychological processes in daily life, capturing within-person dynamics with high temporal resolution (Myin-Germeys et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Momentary Assessment (EMA), enables repeated measurement of psychological processes in daily life, capturing within-person dynamics with high temporal resolution <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Myin-Germeys et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Compared to Routine Outcome Monitoring (ROM) that assesses patient-reported outcomes at regular intervals to track progress and inform clinical decision-making (Barkham et al., 2023), EMA provides a more fine-grained assessment of subjective experiences and behavior in real-world contexts and can be used for self-monitoring, progress tracking, and the evaluation of intervention effects (Myin-Germeys et al., 2024; Piccirillo et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Compared to Routine Outcome Monitoring (ROM) that assesses patient-reported outcomes at regular intervals to track progress and inform clinical decision-making <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Barkham et al., 2023)</ref>, EMA provides a more fine-grained assessment of subjective experiences and behavior in real-world contexts and can be used for self-monitoring, progress tracking, and the evaluation of intervention effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Myin-Germeys et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Piccirillo et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Since ROM-based feedback yields small additive effects (Barkham et al., 2023), EMA may enhance clinical utility by linking psychotherapy more closely to patients' everyday lives and enabling the analysis of within-and between-person processes (Schemer et al., 2023; Wright & Zimmermann, 2019).
text.formatted: Since ROM-based feedback yields small additive effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Barkham et al., 2023)</ref>, EMA may enhance clinical utility by linking psychotherapy more closely to patients' everyday lives and enabling the analysis of within-and between-person processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Schemer et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Wright & Zimmermann, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Building on such intensive longitudinal data, the Network Analysis (NA) approach provides a framework for modeling dynamic psychological systems at the individual level (Roefs et al., 2022), conceptualizing mental disorders as networks of interacting components (e.g., symptoms, behaviors, cognitions; Bringmann et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Building on such intensive longitudinal data, the Network Analysis (NA) approach provides a framework for modeling dynamic psychological systems at the individual level <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(Roefs et al., 2022)</ref>, conceptualizing mental disorders as networks of interacting components (e.g., symptoms, behaviors, cognitions; <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Bringmann et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This system perspective aligns with theoretical accounts emphasizing that psychopathology emerges from dynamic interactions rather than single underlying causes (Borsboom, 2017) and is closely linked to clinical case conceptualization (Scholten et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This system perspective aligns with theoretical accounts emphasizing that psychopathology emerges from dynamic interactions rather than single underlying causes <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Borsboom, 2017)</ref> and is closely linked to clinical case conceptualization <ref type="bibr" target="#b58">(Scholten et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Individual-level networks can inform case conceptualizations by identifying influential processes that may serve as potential treatment targets and guide the prioritization of interventions (Burger et al., 2022; Scholten, Klintwall, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Individual-level networks can inform case conceptualizations by identifying influential processes that may serve as potential treatment targets and guide the prioritization of interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Burger et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Scholten, Klintwall, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This process-oriented perspective is consistent with process-based therapy (S. G. Hofmann & Hayes, 2019), which emphasizes targeting core psychological processes rather than applying standardized treatment protocols based on diagnostic categories.
text.formatted: This process-oriented perspective is consistent with process-based therapy (S. G. <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Hofmann & Hayes, 2019)</ref>, which emphasizes targeting core psychological processes rather than applying standardized treatment protocols based on diagnostic categories.

text.text: First empirical studies provide preliminary support that using network-informed targets may lead to more efficient and potentially more effective treatments (Fisher et al., 2019; Levinson et al., 2023).
text.formatted: First empirical studies provide preliminary support that using network-informed targets may lead to more efficient and potentially more effective treatments <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Fisher et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Levinson et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: At the same time, how network output should be translated into clinical decisions remains unclear.

Target selection typically relies on centrality indices, whose interpretation as indicators of causal influence has been questioned (Bringmann, 2024; Cusack et al., 2025), and person-specific networks depend on choices such as the selected variables and the time scale of measurement.
text.formatted: Target selection typically relies on centrality indices, whose interpretation as indicators of causal influence has been questioned <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bringmann, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Cusack et al., 2025)</ref>, and person-specific networks depend on choices such as the selected variables and the time scale of measurement.

text.text: Some authors have therefore argued that such networks may be more useful as a starting point for collaborative case conceptualization than as prescriptive tools (e.g., von Klipstein et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Some authors have therefore argued that such networks may be more useful as a starting point for collaborative case conceptualization than as prescriptive tools (e.g., von <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Klipstein et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Little is known about how patients and therapists actually use network-based information in treatment.
provide a rigorous methodological framework (Vlaeyen et al., 2022).
text.formatted: provide a rigorous methodological framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Vlaeyen et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: SCEDs involve repeated measurements across baseline and intervention phases allowing individuals to serve as their own control (Schemer et al., 2023).
text.formatted: SCEDs involve repeated measurements across baseline and intervention phases allowing individuals to serve as their own control <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Schemer et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: They have a long tradition in psychological research, particularly in behavior therapy (Barlow et al., 2009; Hayes, 1981) and have regained prominence due to their suitability for evaluating within-person change processes (Vlaeyen et al., 2022).
text.formatted: They have a long tradition in psychological research, particularly in behavior therapy <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Barlow et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Hayes, 1981)</ref> and have regained prominence due to their suitability for evaluating within-person change processes <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Vlaeyen et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In addition to supporting systematic monitoring and evaluation of intervention effects in clinical practice (e.g., Bentley et al., 2019; Simons et al., 2020), SCEDs enable aggregation across cases, thereby strengthening the connection between clinical practice and research and supporting iterative treatment adaptation (Schemer et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In addition to supporting systematic monitoring and evaluation of intervention effects in clinical practice (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">Bentley et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Simons et al., 2020)</ref>, SCEDs enable aggregation across cases, thereby strengthening the connection between clinical practice and research and supporting iterative treatment adaptation <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Schemer et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, these approaches are highly complementary: EMA provides the data basis to model individual dynamics, NA translates these data into data-informed case conceptualizations that can indicate actionable treatment targets, and SCEDs enable the evaluation of resulting interventions within individuals.
Despite this potential, their combined application to guide and evaluate personalized psychotherapy in a coherent framework remains largely unexplored (Berg et al., 2024; Schemer et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Despite this potential, their combined application to guide and evaluate personalized psychotherapy in a coherent framework remains largely unexplored <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Berg et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Schemer et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The present proof-ofconcept study aims to integrate these approaches into a unified framework for data-informed personalized psychotherapy.
The study is conducted in patients with chronic pain; a highly heterogeneous population for whom individualized treatment approaches are particularly warranted (McCracken, 2023).
text.formatted: The study is conducted in patients with chronic pain; a highly heterogeneous population for whom individualized treatment approaches are particularly warranted <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(McCracken, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This study examines the feasibility and acceptability of this approach in clinical practice, explores how patients and therapists experienced the use of network-based information in treatment, and examines its potential to produce meaningful changes in individualized treatment targets and disability measures (V. E. Hofmann et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This study examines the feasibility and acceptability of this approach in clinical practice, explores how patients and therapists experienced the use of network-based information in treatment, and examines its potential to produce meaningful changes in individualized treatment targets and disability measures (V. E. <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Hofmann et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: By combining intensive assessment, data-informed treatment selection, and within-person evaluation, this study seeks to provide an initial test of a Process-Oriented, Individualized, Network-based Therapy for Chronic Pain (POINT-Pain).
Ultimately, the study may serve as a roadmap for the further development and implementation of evidence-based personalized treatments for complex conditions.

The study design was preregistered prospectively on ClinicalTrials, before data were collected (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06179784) and published in a study protocol (V. E. Hofmann et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The study design was preregistered prospectively on ClinicalTrials, before data were collected (<ref type="url" target="https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06179784">https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06179784</ref>) and published in a study protocol (V. E. <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Hofmann et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: It was accepted by the local ethics committee of the psychology department of RPTU University Kaiserslautern-Landau (#LEK-457).

Preliminary treatment effects were evaluated in a Single-Case Experimental Design with four phases (Figure 1): an intensive EMA phase for network estimation (A), a diagnostic phase (B), a randomized baseline phase (C), and an intervention phase (D).
text.formatted: Preliminary treatment effects were evaluated in a Single-Case Experimental Design with four phases (Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref>): an intensive EMA phase for network estimation (A), a diagnostic phase (B), a randomized baseline phase (C), and an intervention phase (D).

text.text: Treatment effects were evaluated by contrasting the baseline (C) and intervention (D) phases, corresponding to an AB phase design with baseline length randomized across participants.

Phase A served for network estimation only and was excluded from effect analyses because of its different assessment frequency; phase B involved clinical contact and therefore did not serve as a baseline.
All participants provided written informed consent before participation.
During phase A, participants completed EMA six times per day for 21 days, with semi-randomized prompts across waking hours.
Person-specific networks were then estimated from these data including up to six variables by mean severity plus up to two more based on patient priorities.
Phase B comprised five weekly sessions including clinical interview, biographical anamnesis, and functional analysis.
Additionally, up to two new idiographic items were formulated with each participant and added to the assessment.
From phase B onward, EMA was reduced to three assessments per week (randomly scheduled on two weekdays and one weekend day) and continued throughout the study.

During the baseline phase (C; one to three weeks, randomized), the treatment target and intervention module were selected in a structured team procedure integrating network results and clinical judgment (see Treatment Planning).
Phase D began with up to two sessions of psychoeducation, followed by up to eight sessions of the selected process-targeted module.
Participants received weekly visual feedback on their data, which was discussed in sessions.
Treatment continued until clinically meaningful improvement in the individualized target was achieved and maintained for at least two weeks, or until the maximum number of sessions was reached.

After the intervention, participants received two monthly booster sessions with continued assessments, followed by a second intensive EMA phase (21 days, six assessments per day) and a threemonth follow-up.
Before proceeding with the study, informed consent was obtained based on a detailed, written study information.

According to the Risk of Bias in N-of-1 Trials Scale (RoBiNT; Tate et al., 2013), the study design reached a conservative risk-of-bias rating of 18 (out of 30 possible) points (see study protocol for further details, V. E. Hofmann et al., 2024).

text.text: The study aimed to recruit 12 adult patients with chronic primary pain (CPP).

For qualitative outcomes, such as feasibility and acceptance, thematic saturation is expected to be achieved with a sample size of approximately 12 participants (Guest et al., 2006; Turner-Bowker et al., 2018).
text.formatted: For qualitative outcomes, such as feasibility and acceptance, thematic saturation is expected to be achieved with a sample size of approximately 12 participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Guest et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Turner-Bowker et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: To evaluate within-person effects, a sample size of n = 1 is sufficient because each individual is analyzed separately.
Inclusion criteria were: age ≥ 18 years, access to a compatible smartphone (Android ≥ 5.1 or iOS ≥ 11.0), a primary diagnosis of CPP (ICD-10: F45.4x), and subjective pain-related disability.

Exclusion criteria comprised acute comorbid conditions requiring immediate treatment (e.g., substance abuse, psychosis, severe underweight, or suicidality), migraine, headache, or neck pain as the primary complaint, insufficient German language proficiency, illiteracy, and physical inability to attend regular outpatient sessions.
Diagnoses and comorbidities were assessed using the German brief version of the Diagnostic Interview for Mental Disorders (Mini-DIPS; Margraf & Cwik, 2020).
text.formatted: Diagnoses and comorbidities were assessed using the German brief version of the Diagnostic Interview for Mental Disorders (Mini-DIPS; <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Margraf & Cwik, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: German language proficiency was assessed via self-report (5-point Likert scale), with scores ≥ 4 indicating insufficient proficiency.
Concurrent participation in other psychotherapy studies or ongoing psychotherapy was not permitted.
All assessments were conducted using m-Path (Mestdagh et al., 2022).
text.formatted: All assessments were conducted using m-Path <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Mestdagh et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: M-Path is a research platform that is flexible and easy to use.
It is used for ambulatory assessment and intensive longitudinal data collection.

Psychological processes were assessed with the German ProCEss item set, developed for the EMA-based assessment of key processes in chronic pain (V. E. Hofmann, Glombiewski, Heider, et al., 2026) and grounded in established models of chronic pain and recommended core outcome domains (Dworkin et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Psychological processes were assessed with the German ProCEss item set, developed for the EMA-based assessment of key processes in chronic pain (V. E. <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Hofmann, Glombiewski, Heider, et al., 2026)</ref> and grounded in established models of chronic pain and recommended core outcome domains <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Dworkin et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Its 25 items cover 14 processes, including pain-related worry, avoidance, depressive symptoms, acceptance, values-based behavior, expectations, thought suppression, task persistence, self-efficacy, self-compassion, positive and negative affect, pain intensity, and pain-related disability.
Items refer to the period since the last assessment and are rated from 0 (not at all) to 10 (completely).
The disability item ("How much did you feel disabled because of your pain?") served as the EMAbased disability outcome.

Patients and clinicians rated the item set as content-valid and clinically useful, and psychometric evaluation indicated adequate within-person variability and generally satisfactory reliability, with lower reliability for self-efficacy, self-compassion, and particularly thought suppression (V. E. Hofmann, Glombiewski, Heider, et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Patients and clinicians rated the item set as content-valid and clinically useful, and psychometric evaluation indicated adequate within-person variability and generally satisfactory reliability, with lower reliability for self-efficacy, self-compassion, and particularly thought suppression (V. E. <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Hofmann, Glombiewski, Heider, et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Patients and therapists completed adapted versions of the System Usability Scale (Gao et al., 2020) and the User Experience Questionnaire -Short Version (UEQ-S; Schrepp et al., 2017) to evaluate the usability of the m-Path app and the associated presentation of the study results.
text.formatted: Patients and therapists completed adapted versions of the System Usability Scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Gao et al., 2020)</ref> and the User Experience Questionnaire -Short Version (UEQ-S; <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Schrepp et al., 2017)</ref> to evaluate the usability of the m-Path app and the associated presentation of the study results.

text.text: (Details regarding SUS and UEQ are reported in the Supplementary Material S1.3 Measures, Feasibility Outcomes).
Feasibility was evaluated via compliance rates with the assessment protocol across study phases.
A compliance rate of ≥ 80% was considered indicative of good feasibility.
Acceptance was assessed using qualitative interviews, quantitative questionnaires, and compliance rates.
Semi-structured interviews were conducted with patients and therapists as the final assessment of the study to explore expectations, usability, and perceived utility of the intervention components.

Core domains included expectations, study onboarding, app usability, assessment burden (e.g., EMA frequency), feasibility of the study procedure, perceived utility of the intervention components, and potential negative effects.
Interviews also addressed the comprehensibility and usefulness of person-specific networks and the acceptance of algorithm-guided intervention selection.
Therapists were additionally asked about the clarity and clinical utility of the presentation of the results.
Each participant was assigned to one of ten intervention modules in a structured team procedure, the Algorithm-Guided Intervention Selection Team (AGIST; Figure 2).
text.formatted: Each participant was assigned to one of ten intervention modules in a structured team procedure, the Algorithm-Guided Intervention Selection Team (AGIST; Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: First, the study therapist, supervisor, and researcher developed a shared case conceptualization from the diagnostic information without knowledge of the network results and documented the modules they considered suitable.

The researcher then presented the network-derived treatment target (the variable with the highest mean of contemporaneous strength and temporal out-strength; Rubel et al., 2018) and the two modules recommended by a predefined matching matrix (V. E. Hofmann, Glombiewski, & Scholten, 2026).
text.formatted: The researcher then presented the network-derived treatment target (the variable with the highest mean of contemporaneous strength and temporal out-strength; <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Rubel et al., 2018)</ref> and the two modules recommended by a predefined matching matrix (V. E. <ref type="bibr">Hofmann, Glombiewski, & Scholten, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The primary recommendation was adopted unless adverse effects were anticipated, in which case the alternative module was chosen.
The selected module was discussed with the patient and delivered throughout the intervention phase; reassignment in supervision was possible in case of adverse effects or sustained non-response.

The ten modules were derived from cognitive-behavioral and third-wave treatments for chronic pain and adapted from established treatment manuals: exposure in vivo, relaxation, activity pacing, cognitive coping, attention control, resource activation, acceptance, values-based action, sleep, and self-compassion (see S1.1, Table S1).
text.formatted: The ten modules were derived from cognitive-behavioral and third-wave treatments for chronic pain and adapted from established treatment manuals: exposure in vivo, relaxation, activity pacing, cognitive coping, attention control, resource activation, acceptance, values-based action, sleep, and self-compassion (see S1.1, Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref>).

text.text: After one or two sessions of psychoeducation and motivational support, depending on patients' prior knowledge, each module followed the same four-part sequence: (1) developing an individual disorder model and treatment rationale, (2) individual diagnostics and problem definition, (3) implementation, and (4) consolidation, with the length of each part adapted to the patient.
Homework was reviewed at the start of each session, and patients received weekly feedback on their progress based on their SCED plots.
Each week during therapy, therapists received a visual feedback report displaying the patient's target item over time.

The report included a line plot depicting repeated measurements of the target variable across the different study phases, with phase transitions visually marked to facilitate interpretation of change over time.

In addition, quantitative feedback regarding treatment effects was provided using the TAU-BC statistic and the Bayes Factor to support evaluation of changes associated with the intervention (de Vries et al., 2015; Tarlow, 2017).
text.formatted: In addition, quantitative feedback regarding treatment effects was provided using the TAU-BC statistic and the Bayes Factor to support evaluation of changes associated with the intervention <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(de Vries et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Tarlow, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Therapists were instructed to review and discuss the feedback with patients at the beginning of each therapy session and to integrate the results into the ongoing therapeutic process.
Before treatment, all study therapists completed a workshop on SCED and personspecific network analysis.
During therapy, therapists received supervision at least every fourth session.

Treatment fidelity was assessed with a module-specific adherence checklist derived from the treatment manual and expert review (e.g., Leeuw et al., 2009), covering unique, permitted, and prohibited elements of each module as well as whether EMA feedback and the treatment rationale were discussed (see S1.2).
text.formatted: Treatment fidelity was assessed with a module-specific adherence checklist derived from the treatment manual and expert review (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Leeuw et al., 2009)</ref>, covering unique, permitted, and prohibited elements of each module as well as whether EMA feedback and the treatment rationale were discussed (see S1.2).

text.text: Two independent raters not involved in treatment delivery rated four video-recorded sessions per patient spanning all therapy phases and judged whether the assigned module had been delivered as intended (adherent vs. nonadherent; interrater reliability: Cohen's κ; J. Cohen, 1960)).
text.formatted: Two independent raters not involved in treatment delivery rated four video-recorded sessions per patient spanning all therapy phases and judged whether the assigned module had been delivered as intended (adherent vs. nonadherent; interrater reliability: Cohen's κ; J. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Cohen, 1960)</ref>).

text.text: In addition, therapists documented the interventions used after each session (self-rated fidelity).
Analyses followed the published study protocol (V. E. Hofmann et al., 2024), which specified visual analysis, baseline-corrected Tau, and Hedges' g for the evaluation of individual treatment effects.
text.formatted: Analyses followed the published study protocol (V. E. <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Hofmann et al., 2024)</ref>, which specified visual analysis, baseline-corrected Tau, and Hedges' g for the evaluation of individual treatment effects.

text.text: Within-person regression models and a multilevel model of average treatment effects were conducted in addition and should be considered exploratory.

Further exploratory analyses not specified in the protocol (Bayes factors and comparisons of pre-and post-treatment networks) and descriptive results for secondary outcomes are reported in the Supplementary Material (S1.5, S1.7, S1.8, S2.5, S2.6, S2.7).
The qualitative analysis was preregistered separately (V. E. Hofmann, Glombiewski, & Scholten, 2026).
text.formatted: The qualitative analysis was preregistered separately (V. E. <ref type="bibr">Hofmann, Glombiewski, & Scholten, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions, all manipulations, and all measures in the study.
All analyses were conducted in R (R Development Core Team, 2025; version 4.6.0) within RStudio (Posit, 2025; version 2026.04.0+526).
text.formatted: All analyses were conducted in R (R Development Core Team, 2025; version 4.6.0) within RStudio <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Posit, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr">version 2026</ref>.04.0+526).

text.text: Several packages for data management, visualization, and statistical analysis (see S1.10).
Missing observations and exclusions were handled separately for each analysis as described below.
Descriptive statistics (mean, median, standard deviation) were calculated for each EMA variable.
Positively valenced items (e.g., positive affect, acceptance) were recoded where necessary to ensure consistent directionality across variables.
Variable selection followed predefined criteria to improve robustness of individual network estimation.

text.text: Of these, N = 15 participants were enrolled in the study.
During the study, N = 3 participants discontinued participation, resulting in a final sample of N = 12 participants included in the analyses.
Data collection was completed in August 2025.
A detailed overview of participant flow is provided in the Supplementary Material S2.1.
The final sample consisted of N = 12 participants with chronic primary pain (see S2.2 Sociodemographic characteristics of the patients, Table S2).

text.text: Participants had a mean age of M = 60.25 years (SD = 7.2, range = 54-80).
All participants met criteria for chronic primary pain (ICD-10: F45.41).
Comorbid mental disorders were present in n = 5 participants, with the most frequent diagnoses being depressive disorders (n = 5).
Therapists had a mean age of 32.3 years (range: 26-39) and were predominantly female (n = 7), with two male therapists.
Two therapists were fully licensed, while seven were in clinical training.
Most had between 0 and 5 years of professional experience (n = 7), with three reporting 6-10 years and one reporting 11-15 years of experience.
Three therapists treated two patients each.
Overall, the assessment protocol resulted in 3580 observations with an average of 298 (Min: 188; Max: 376) observations per person.
Compliance ranged from 24 -100% with high variations across phases (A: 73-98%; B: 55-100%; C: 50-100%; D: 45-100%; second intensive EMA phase: 24-97%).

Overall, at least seven patients reached the pre-defined criterion of 80% compliance in every phase, with a maximum of 11 patients reaching 80% in the diagnostic phase and in the post-treatment EMA phase.
In the clinical case conceptualization, conducted without knowledge of the network results, the clinical team identified up to three suitable modules per patient.
These overlapped with at least one of the two algorithm-recommended modules in 6 of 13 cases (46%) and with both in two cases.
The clinical team's first choice matched an algorithm-recommended module in only two cases.
The primary recommendation was adopted in 12 cases, and the alternative module was chosen in 1 case because adverse effects were anticipated.
No module was reassigned during treatment.
Interrater agreement for the global adherence judgment was substantial (Cohen's κ = .63).
Both raters judged 10 of 12 treatments as adherent; one treatment was rated adherent by only one rater, and one was rated non-adherent by both.
Therapists self-reported deviations from the assigned module in three treatments.
Agreement between external ratings and therapists' self-reports was slight (Fleiss' κ = .16).
Visual analysis indicated consistent improvement in level and trend in six participants, mixed patterns in three, and deterioration in three (see S2.3).
Baseline-Corrected TAU did not indicate significant change for any participant (Table 1).

text.text: Patients and therapists rated the usability of the m-Path app and of the presentation of results (network and feedback plots) on the System Usability Scale (SUS; range 0-100).
The app received high ratings from patients (M = 85.19, SD = 16.81) and above-average ratings from therapists (M = 69.44, SD = 22.90).
The presentation of results was rated lower, particularly by therapists (patients: M = 79.23, SD = 18.21; therapists: M = 53.06, SD = 16.29).
On the User Experience Questionnaire (UEQ-S; range -3 to 3), hedonic quality was positive for patients (M = 1.54, SD = 1.29) and therapists (M = 1.00, SD = 0.84).
Pragmatic quality was lower and exceeded the threshold for a positive evaluation (> 0.8; Schrepp et al., 2017) among patients (M = 0.87, SD = 0.59) but not among therapists (M = 0.64, SD = 0.64).

text.text: Rater agreement for assigning paraphrases to research questions was good (patients: κ = .76; therapists: κ = .83).
The complete category system with example quotes is provided in the Supplementary Material S2.8.
Patients and therapists described POINT-Pain as a structured, yet flexible framework integrated into ongoing psychotherapy.
Both groups experienced the data visualizations as orientation that helped maintain therapeutic focus and supported treatment decisions.

Network and feedback plots were discussed in sessions and served as a starting point for reflecting on symptom relations and treatment targets; therapists used the network to explain treatment rationales, and patients appreciated that planning was guided by data rather than intuition alone.
Patients also engaged with their data between sessions.
Deviations from the protocol, such as irregular use of feedback, were attributed to practical barriers, forgetfulness, or difficulties understanding the visualizations.
Perceived effects and mechanisms.
Perceived effects ranged from reduced symptoms and improved functioning to a better understanding of pain and increased self-awareness.
However, some participants reported little or no change (e.g., Therapist: "I don't really have much hope that much has changed."
; Patient: "The pain is still there."
; Negative side effects and non-response), and some patients experienced the frequent assessments as burdensome reminders of their pain.

Both groups attributed change to factors such as the therapeutic relationship, to the structured, goal-oriented treatment process, and to repeated selfobservation and personalized feedback, which increased awareness of everyday patterns and created opportunities for reflection.
For example, one therapist described "refram[ing] it and manag [ing] to get the curve after all," while a patient explained that therapy focused on improving interpersonal functioning.
text.formatted: For example, one therapist described "refram[ing] it and manag <ref type="bibr">[ing]</ref> to get the curve after all," while a patient explained that therapy focused on improving interpersonal functioning.

text.text: Some therapists could not attribute change to a specific component, and patients also named contextual factors such as concurrent physiotherapy.
Therapists additionally reported professional learning, including a more structured and goaloriented approach.
For example, one therapist stated, "For me, self-compassion hadn't even crossed my mind before," while another reflected, "I learned a lot about pain."
Facilitators and barriers.
Therapists described facilitators and barriers in similar measure, whereas patients reported more barriers.

Experiences varied considerably between participants and often reflected opposite poles of the same issue, such as "Formulating idiographic items was easy." and "I realized that I didn't have many ideas either, so only very lackluster ideas emerged, which were harder to put into words [idiographic items]."
Participants emphasized understandable item wording, addressing initial concerns, technical support, training and supervision, and a balance between structure and flexibility (see S2.9).

This proof-of-concept study examined how Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) based monitoring, person-specific networks, and modular evidence-based interventions can be integrated into data-informed personalized treatment for chronic pain, and how such an approach functions in clinical practice.

The approach proved largely feasible: patients provided a mean of 298 observations, and treatments were mostly delivered as intended, although three of 15 patients discontinued and not all participants met the compliance criterion in every phase.
Preliminary effects were mixed.
Disability decreased on average, but individual trajectories ranged from improvement to deterioration.
Patients and therapists primarily valued the self-monitoring and structured, data-informed reflection the approach enabled.
At the same time, participant burden, the interpretability of the network output, and the balance between structure and flexibility emerged as areas for improvement.
Designing this approach highlighted several unresolved questions along the individual-level clinical decision-making pathway (Scholten & Glombiewski, 2025).
text.formatted: Designing this approach highlighted several unresolved questions along the individual-level clinical decision-making pathway <ref type="bibr">(Scholten & Glombiewski, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We discuss these along the three steps of the framework: observing, deciding, and intervening.
Patients experienced the intensive EMA phase as burdensome yet missed it once assessments were reduced to three per week.
This suggests a non-linear trade-off between burden and perceived informational value.

Rather than a universal sampling rate, the findings support flexible, hybrid monitoring architectures that combine measurement bursts to capture short-term dynamics (Andresen et al., 2025), moderate-frequency monitoring to inform case formulation, and lower-frequency Routine Outcome Monitoring (ROM) to track progress (Barkham et al., 2023), with assessment design treated as an iterative clinical decision.
text.formatted: Rather than a universal sampling rate, the findings support flexible, hybrid monitoring architectures that combine measurement bursts to capture short-term dynamics <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Andresen et al., 2025)</ref>, moderate-frequency monitoring to inform case formulation, and lower-frequency Routine Outcome Monitoring (ROM) to track progress <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Barkham et al., 2023)</ref>, with assessment design treated as an iterative clinical decision.

text.text: Beyond data collection, patients and therapists described self-monitoring as an active part of therapy that increased awareness of everyday patterns and brought daily-life experiences into sessions.
EMA may thus function not only as assessment infrastructure but as a processsupporting intervention element (Bos et al., 2022; Piccirillo et al., 2026; Scholten et al., 2026).
text.formatted: EMA may thus function not only as assessment infrastructure but as a processsupporting intervention element <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Bos et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Piccirillo et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Scholten et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The most direct evidence on how network-based recommendations function in practice comes from comparing them with clinical judgment.

The modules selected by the clinical team without knowledge of the network results overlapped with the algorithmic recommendations in fewer than half of the cases, and the team's first choice matched an algorithm-recommended module in only two cases.
The networks thus did not merely confirm clinicians' formulations but introduced a different perspective.
Whether this perspective was more accurate cannot be determined from the present data.

Disagreement may stem from target selection as well as from the matching matrix, which, for instance, assigned the same modules whenever disability was the target, whereas clinicians chose different modules in each of these cases.
Based on these findings, we have revised the matching matrix (V. E. Hofmann, Glombiewski, & Scholten, 2026).
text.formatted: Based on these findings, we have revised the matching matrix (V. E. <ref type="bibr">Hofmann, Glombiewski, & Scholten, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Because the decision rule permitted deviations only when adverse effects were anticipated, the primary recommendation was adopted in 12 of 13 cases, and treatment selection was therefore largely algorithm-driven.
The value of the Algorithm-Guided Intervention Seletion Team (AGIST) thus lay less in changing decisions than in the reflection it prompted.

Therapists described it as a particularly valuable space for reflecting on decisions, clarifying patient aims, and making intervention choices transparent, and both groups used the networks to explain treatment rationales.

At the same time, therapists rated the usability of the network output below average, some participants found the visualizations difficult to understand, and both patients and therapists raised ethical concerns about data-driven decisions.
Together, these findings suggest that the clinical value of the network approach does not depend on statistical accuracy alone.
Its primary contribution may lie in providing a structured language for representing interactions between symptoms, experiences, and behaviors that supports collaborative case conceptualization.

In this sense, simplified or qualitatively derived perceived causal networks may be sufficient, or in some cases preferable (Vogel et al., 2025), and hybrid approaches combining patient knowledge, clinical expertise, and empirical data may strengthen this translational step (Burger et al., 2022; Scholten, Klintwall, et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In this sense, simplified or qualitatively derived perceived causal networks may be sufficient, or in some cases preferable <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Vogel et al., 2025)</ref>, and hybrid approaches combining patient knowledge, clinical expertise, and empirical data may strengthen this translational step <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Burger et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Scholten, Klintwall, et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The study also underscored the role of patient goals.

Monitoring personally defined goals provides a stable reference point for evaluating progress (Cooper & Xu, 2023; Weisz et al., 2011), whereas dynamically assessed variables can be understood as potential mechanisms influencing goal attainment.
text.formatted: Monitoring personally defined goals provides a stable reference point for evaluating progress <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Cooper & Xu, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Weisz et al., 2011)</ref>, whereas dynamically assessed variables can be understood as potential mechanisms influencing goal attainment.

text.text: Goals, mechanisms, and interventions may thus be viewed as complementary levels of clinical reasoning (the destination, the terrain, and the route) rather than a linear sequence.
Delivering one selected module was experienced as focused, facilitating patients' transfer of coping strategies into daily life and therapists' procedural competence.
However, patients perceived the module as too long, therapists experienced limited flexibility, and both noted conceptual overlap between modules.

The slight agreement between external fidelity ratings and therapists' self-reports suggests that therapists may have adapted the procedure more than they recognized or reported, a further indication of the tension between structure and flexibility.
Future research should examine the specific and shared effects of modules, their optimal dosage, and sequencing (Mulder et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Future research should examine the specific and shared effects of modules, their optimal dosage, and sequencing <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Mulder et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: The preliminary effects should be interpreted in this light.
Disability decreased on average, but no individual BC-Tau estimate was significant, and two participants deteriorated significantly on their target.
With baselines of only 3-12 observations, individual-level analyses had limited power and precision, so nonsignificant results do not indicate an absence of change.
The deteriorations nevertheless warrant attentionP2 experienced several stressful life events during treatment that therapy could not sufficiently address.

For P4, post hoc case discussions in the study team suggested that the increase in ignoring pain was functional for this patient as it enabled engagement in valued activities, which the item formulation did not capture.
This illustrates that the direction of change on a single EMA item cannot be interpreted without clinical context.

In addition, patients described meaningful changes, such as new perspectives and coping strategies, that the outcome measures did not capture (De Smet et al., 2020), and therapists expressed a need for clearer guidelines for translating weekly SCED feedback into clinical decisions, comparable to established ROM systems (e.g., Barkham et al., 2023; Lutz et al., 2022).
text.formatted: In addition, patients described meaningful changes, such as new perspectives and coping strategies, that the outcome measures did not capture <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(De Smet et al., 2020)</ref>, and therapists expressed a need for clearer guidelines for translating weekly SCED feedback into clinical decisions, comparable to established ROM systems (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Barkham et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Lutz et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Strengths of the study include its mixed-methods design combining patient and therapist perspectives, a published protocol, external fidelity ratings, and the blinded clinical case conceptualization, which allowed a direct comparison of clinical and algorithmic treatment selection.
Several limitations concern the approach itself.

Person-specific networks remain methodologically contested with regard to the reliability of time-varying data, construct validity, the stability of estimates, and the use of centrality indices for target selection (Bringmann, 2024; Cusack et al., 2025; Scholten et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025)
text.formatted: Person-specific networks remain methodologically contested with regard to the reliability of time-varying data, construct validity, the stability of estimates, and the use of centrality indices for target selection <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bringmann, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Cusack et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Scholten et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Zhang et al., 2025)</ref>

text.text: Personalized psychotherapy may benefit from being conceptualized not as the application of isolated individualized techniques but as a recursive cycle in which observation informs decisions, decisions guide interventions, and interventions generate new data that refine subsequent understanding.

From this perspective, the clinical value of data-informed personalization may lie less in algorithmic precision than in its capacity to raise awareness, structure reflection, enhance shared understanding, and support the iterative updating of clinicians' and patients' beliefs about the therapeutic process (Herzog et al., 2023).
text.formatted: From this perspective, the clinical value of data-informed personalization may lie less in algorithmic precision than in its capacity to raise awareness, structure reflection, enhance shared understanding, and support the iterative updating of clinicians' and patients' beliefs about the therapeutic process <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Herzog et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Future developments should therefore focus not only on methodological sophistication but also on the interpretability, flexibility, and clinical usability of personalized psychotherapy frameworks in routine care.

Moreover, the networks captured hour-to-hour dynamics (lag-1 at six assessments per day), whereas treatment progress was evaluated week to week; processes at one time scale do not necessarily drive change at another.

It also remains unclear which components of the framework (EMA, network modeling, intervention selection, or SCED-based feedback) contributed to the observed changes, or whether benefits emerge from their combination.
Finally, the framework focuses on intra-individual dynamics, whereas change also unfolds within biological, social, and environmental contexts (von Klipstein et al., 2025).

Methodological limitations include a moderate risk of bias (RoBiNT: 18 of 30 points; V. E. Hofmann et al., 2024) due to nonconcurrent baselines, incomplete blinding, and the absence of systematic replication across phases, which limits causal inference.
Because of limited resources, members of the research team served as therapists in four cases, which may have compromised blinding and treatment fidelity.
Autocorrelation was not modeled in the regression and multilevel analyses, and the network invariance test could not be interpreted for seven of twelve participants.
Finally, the small sample, three dropouts, and the idiographic nature of the data limit generalizability.
Future studies should separate clinical and research roles, use replication-focused designs, and include more diverse samples.
